title: Supatipanno
hookLine: palms together at the chest: a greeting the sangha verse ends with
tomorrow: how many Pali words do you already know? more than you think.

cards: Hands talk before mouths do. A fist bump, a hand on the heart, a wave across a parking lot.
In a Lao or Thai temple, the greeting is palms pressed together at the chest, often with a small bow, and you'll see a grandfather do it to a monk young enough to be his grandson.
So who comes third, after the Buddha and his teaching? Not one person. A community, the sangha.
And the verse that praises it ends in the hands.

teach.b: It opens: supatipanno bhagavato savakasangho. The Blessed One's community of disciples is practicing well. Then three more lines, each a way of walking.
Uju is straight, like a spine that isn't slumped or a road with no detours. Nayapatipanno: practicing the true way. Samicipatipanno: practicing properly.
Notice what gets praised. Not robes, not age, not titles. A verb, four times over: practicing.
The verse even says whom it means: those walking the path of awakening and those who have arrived.

Then come the reasons to honor them: worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, and anjalikaraniyo, worthy of anjali, joined palms. That's why the grandfather bows to the young monk.
He isn't bowing to a birthday. He's bowing to the practice. And the verse closes by calling this community an unsurpassed field of merit for the world: good planted there grows.

how: Theravada Buddhists chant the sangha verse after the verses on the Buddha and the dhamma, and greet monks and nuns with anjali, palms joined at the chest, often with a bow.

o: walking the Buddhist path well, the way the sangha does
the bow a student makes when entering a shrine hall
a monk's long years of seniority in the temple

games.q: the sangha verse — tap the pairs.

s: in the temple, the oldest person is the one everyone bows to
the verse honors the sangha for practicing well; a grandfather may bow to a young monk.
anjali, joined palms, is named inside the sangha verse itself
anjalikaraniyo: worthy of anjali, the joined palms.
the verse praises the sangha for its robes and rituals
it praises a verb, four times: practicing well, straight, the true way, properly.

games.q: your meditation group has two newcomers. one quotes Pali and wears fancy retreat clothes. the other shows up every week and quietly helps stack the cushions. by the sangha verse, what's worth honoring?
o: the Pali and the clothes: they show who's serious.
how each one actually practices, straight, true and properly.
neither, until they've been around for years.
games.why: the verse praises practicing: well, straight, the true way, properly. looks, words and time served aren't on its list.

practice: Sit up straight, uju, as if a thread lifted the top of your head, and press your palms together at your chest. Chant the opening line once: supatipanno bhagavato savakasangho.
Then let your hands rest in your lap, keep the straight back for the sit, and feel the warmth stay in your palms.

wordCard.voice: Supatipanno: practicing well. The first word of the sangha verse, which honors a community for how it walks the path.

orig.note: Pali, in Devanagari letters: su, well, and patipanno, practicing, walking the path.

carryVoice: Keep this one: practicing well, straight, true and properly, at any age. Twenty days into Pali now.

sources.ref: SN 11.3 (Dhajagga Sutta): the qualities of the sangha, supatipanno bhagavato savakasangho … anuttaram punnakkhettam lokassa
Recollection of the sangha (sanghanussati): ujupatipanno, nayapatipanno, samicipatipanno; ahuneyyo, pahuneyyo, dakkhineyyo, anjalikaraniyo
sources.work: Pali formula, as in DN 16 and AN 6.10
